stem: An organisation publishes an SPF record listing its mail servers. Attackers continue to send messages whose visible From address is the company's domain, and recipients still accept them. Why does SPF not stop this?

options.text: SPF validates the envelope sender's IP, not the From header the recipient reads, so a forged From passes untouched
options.why: This is the gap DMARC exists to close. SPF can pass for a message whose visible sender is entirely fabricated, because it never looks at that header.

options.text: SPF records only take effect once DKIM signing is enabled
options.why: They are independent. SPF works on its own; it simply checks something other than what the user sees.

options.text: The SPF record must be published as a CNAME rather than a TXT record
options.why: SPF is published as a DNS TXT record. The record type is not the issue.

options.text: SPF only applies to inbound mail, not outbound
options.why: You publish SPF so other receivers can check mail claiming to be from you. Direction is not the problem.

stem: Which statement correctly describes what DMARC adds beyond SPF and DKIM?

options.text: It requires that an SPF or DKIM pass align with the visible From domain, and tells receivers what to do when that fails
options.why: DMARC performs no check of its own. It adds alignment and a published policy of none, quarantine or reject, plus aggregate reporting back to the domain owner.

options.text: It encrypts the message in transit between mail servers
options.why: That is TLS, negotiated by STARTTLS. DMARC is about authentication and policy, not confidentiality.

options.text: It performs a third independent check of the sending server's identity
options.why: There is no third check. DMARC consumes the results of the other two and judges alignment.

options.text: It signs outbound messages so recipients can verify integrity
options.why: Signing is DKIM. DMARC references the DKIM result rather than producing one.

stem: A message arrives with a valid DKIM signature from partner-domain.example and was delivered over an opportunistically encrypted connection. What has been established?

options.text: The message was signed by that domain and was not modified after signing; the encryption protected it only between those two servers
options.why: DKIM gives origin authentication and integrity for the signed parts. STARTTLS protects a hop, not the message, so it says nothing about any earlier or later relay.

options.text: The message was encrypted end to end from sender to recipient
options.why: Transport encryption covers one connection at a time. Each relay decrypts and re-encrypts, and opportunistic means it can silently fall back to plaintext.

options.text: The visible From address is guaranteed to belong to that domain
options.why: Only if DMARC alignment is checked. DKIM alone can be valid for a signing domain that differs from the one shown to the user.

options.text: The sending server's IP address is authorised for that domain
options.why: That is SPF's check. DKIM is indifferent to which IP sent the message.

stem: Most staff now work from home and connect directly to the internet without a VPN. Which web filtering approach maintains policy enforcement for them?

options.text: An agent-based filter installed on each device
options.why: The agent travels with the laptop, so enforcement does not depend on traffic returning to a corporate egress point.

options.text: A centralised proxy at the head office
options.why: A proxy only filters what is routed through it. Direct internet traffic from home never reaches it.

options.text: Firewall rules on the corporate perimeter
options.why: Same problem: the perimeter is not in the path for a device browsing from home.

options.text: A screened subnet for the published web applications
options.why: That concerns inbound access to your services, not outbound browsing by staff.

stem: Users are being directed to domains registered within the last 48 hours that host credential harvesting pages. The domains have no category yet and are not on any block list. Which filtering mechanism addresses this best?

options.text: Reputation-based filtering, which can act on domain age and hosting signals before a category exists
options.why: Reputation scores exist precisely for destinations nothing yet knows anything about. Newly registered domain is one of the strongest signals available.

options.text: Content categorisation
options.why: Categorisation needs the site to have been assessed and classified. A 48-hour-old domain has not been.

options.text: Explicit block rules for the offending domains
options.why: Reactive by nature: you can only block what you already know, and the attacker registers new domains faster than you list them.

options.text: URL scanning of the full path
options.why: Useful for a page on a known host, but it still needs some basis for judging a host nobody has seen before.

stem: A business needs to allow a widely used file sharing service but block one specific folder path on it that is being abused. The organisation currently uses DNS filtering. What is the limitation?

options.text: DNS filtering resolves at the domain level, so it can only allow or block the whole service, not one path within it
options.why: DNS answers a name query. It never sees the path, which is why path-level decisions need a proxy or an agent that can inspect the URL.

options.text: DNS filtering cannot block any destination that uses HTTPS
options.why: It blocks by refusing to resolve the name, which works regardless of the protocol that would have followed.

options.text: DNS filtering requires an agent on each endpoint to function
options.why: It works by pointing clients at a filtering resolver. No agent is required, which is part of its appeal.

options.text: DNS filtering only applies to inbound traffic
options.why: It governs outbound name resolution by internal clients.

stem: An organisation is breached using a technique with no published signature. Its IDS, configured purely for signature-based detection, recorded nothing. Which change would most likely have detected it?

options.text: Adding trend and anomaly-based detection against a behavioural baseline
options.why: Anomaly detection does not need to know the attack. It needs to know normal, and flags deviation, which is the only route to catching something previously unseen.

options.text: Updating the signature database more frequently
options.why: No frequency helps when no signature exists for the technique anywhere.

options.text: Moving the IDS from a tap to an inline position
options.why: Inline placement lets it block rather than merely alert. It does not improve what it can recognise.

options.text: Lowering the alert threshold on existing signatures
options.why: That produces more alerts from the signatures you have, none of which match this traffic.

stem: A team deploys anomaly-based detection and establishes its baseline over two weeks. Investigators later determine the network was already compromised throughout that period. What is the consequence?

options.text: The attacker's traffic was learned as normal, so the very behaviour that should alert is now the baseline
options.why: Behavioural detection is only as good as the period it learned from. Baselining a compromised environment trains the system to accept the intrusion.

options.text: The baseline is unaffected, because anomaly detection ignores malicious traffic when learning
options.why: It has no way to tell malicious from normal while learning. That judgement is what it is trying to acquire.

options.text: Signature detection would have had the same problem
options.why: Signatures come from an external database and are unaffected by what your network was doing during setup.

options.text: The baseline will self-correct within a few days of normal traffic
options.why: Not without re-baselining deliberately. The malicious pattern is embedded in what the system considers normal.

stem: A web service running as root on a Linux host is exploited. The attacker's code cannot read files outside the web content directories, even though it holds root privileges. Which control produced this result?

options.text: SELinux enforcing mandatory access control by label
options.why: Mandatory access control sits above the account. A process confined by its label is bound by policy regardless of running as root, which is the entire reason it exists.

options.text: Group Policy restricting the service account
options.why: Group Policy is a Windows mechanism delivered through Active Directory. It does not apply to a Linux host.

options.text: Discretionary access control through file permissions
options.why: Under DAC root overrides file permissions. Something above the account had to be enforcing this.

options.text: The principle of least privilege applied to the service account
options.why: Least privilege would have meant not running as root at all. The scenario states it was root and still confined.

stem: An administrator must apply a consistent password policy, screen lock timeout and software restriction to four thousand domain-joined Windows workstations. Which capability is designed for this?

options.text: Group Policy
options.why: Centralised distribution of configuration and security settings to domain members is precisely what Group Policy does, and at that scale nothing manual is viable.

options.text: SELinux policy modules
options.why: SELinux is a Linux kernel mechanism and has no presence on Windows workstations.

options.text: Network access control posture checks
options.why: NAC can test whether a device meets a posture before admitting it. It does not configure the setting in the first place.

options.text: Endpoint detection and response policies
options.why: EDR observes and responds to activity. It is not a configuration management mechanism.

stem: A web server is compromised and the attacker quietly replaces a configuration file to add a redirect. No data leaves the host and no account behaves unusually. Which capability is designed to catch this?

options.text: File integrity monitoring
options.why: FIM baselines specific files by hash and alerts on unexpected change. When the attack is a quiet modification rather than an exfiltration, it is the control that sees it.

options.text: Data loss prevention
options.why: DLP watches sensitive content moving. Nothing is being sent out in this scenario.

options.text: User behaviour analytics
options.why: UBA baselines account behaviour. The stem explicitly says no account behaved unusually.

options.text: Network access control
options.why: NAC governs which devices may join the network. The server is already legitimately connected.

stem: An employee who has resigned uploads a spreadsheet of customer contact details to a personal cloud account during working hours, from their normal device and at their normal time. Which capability most directly detects this?

options.text: Data loss prevention, which inspects content and blocks sensitive data leaving by policy
options.why: Everything about the behaviour is normal except what is inside the file. Only a content-aware control catches that.

options.text: User behaviour analytics
options.why: UBA looks for deviation from a baseline, and this user is deviating from nothing: same device, same hours, same pattern.

options.text: File integrity monitoring on the file server
options.why: FIM alerts on files changing. Reading a file and uploading a copy changes nothing.

options.text: Endpoint detection and response
options.why: EDR looks for malicious execution. A browser uploading a file is ordinary endpoint activity.

stem: A finance account signs in at 03:40 from an unfamiliar country, accesses systems it has never touched, and does so while the employee is on leave. Which TWO capabilities are most relevant? (Choose two.)

options.text: User behaviour analytics, which flags an account behaving unlike itself and unlike its peers
options.why: Time, location and unusual resource access are the signals UBA is built on. Nothing about the content matters here.

options.text: Data loss prevention, if the session then moves sensitive data out
options.why: UBA detects the anomalous access; DLP is what stands between that session and the data leaving. They cover different halves.

options.text: File integrity monitoring on the finance workstation
options.why: No protected file is being altered, and the activity is not on that workstation.

options.text: Network access control
options.why: NAC admits or refuses devices at the door. This is a remote session with valid credentials.

options.text: Agent-based web filtering
options.why: Web filtering governs which sites users may reach, not anomalous use of an internal account.
